summary:
Dancing with the SARs is an AI-powered disaster monitoring and landslide risk assessment platform designed to improve disaster preparedness in Uttarakhand's Himalayan region. It leverages NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) satellite data to monitor Earth's surface changes and study environmental hazards such as landslides, ground deformation, floods, and glacier movement.

The platform integrates SAR observations with environmental datasets, including rainfall information and Digital Elevation Models (DEM), to analyze geographical and climatic conditions. Using machine learning, it processes relevant features to estimate landslide susceptibility and generate location-based risk assessments.

Users can select a geographical location and observation date to explore available satellite observations, visualize terrain conditions, and understand potential risk levels through interactive maps and dashboards. It transforms complex satellite data into accessible insights for researchers, disaster management authorities, and local communities.

Built using Python, FastAPI, Next.js, React, TypeScript, Three.js, and Supabase, the platform combines geospatial processing, machine learning, and interactive 3D visualization.

Our vision is to make satellite intelligence accessible and actionable, supporting early risk identification, better disaster preparedness, and informed decision-making in vulnerable Himalayan communities.
details:
Project Description – Dancing with the SARs

Dancing with the SARs is an AI-powered geospatial disaster monitoring and landslide risk assessment platform developed for the Himalayan region of Uttarakhand, India. The project uses satellite-based Earth observation data, particularly from the NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission, to understand changes in Earth's surface and support disaster preparedness.

How Does It Work?

The platform allows users to select a geographical location and observation date. It retrieves available satellite observations and combines them with environmental datasets such as rainfall and Digital Elevation Models (DEM). These datasets are processed to extract relevant geographical features, which are then analyzed using machine learning models to estimate landslide susceptibility and generate location-specific risk levels. The results are presented through interactive maps, dashboards, and 3D terrain visualizations.

Benefits and Intended Impact

  • Supports early identification of potentially vulnerable areas.
  • Helps disaster management authorities make informed decisions.
  • Makes complex satellite and geospatial data easier to understand.
  • Supports researchers and local communities in understanding environmental risks.
  • Promotes disaster preparedness and climate resilience in mountainous regions.

Tools and Technologies Used

  • Programming Languages: Python, JavaScript, TypeScript.
  • Backend: FastAPI, Python.
  • Frontend: Next.js 14, React, Three.js.
  • Database: Supabase.
  • Cloud Storage: Cloudflare R2.
  • Data Sources: NASA-ISRO NISAR, NASA Earthdata, rainfall datasets, and Digital Elevation Models.
  • Machine Learning: Python-based geospatial data processing and predictive modeling.

Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of Dancing with the SARs is its approach to transforming complex satellite radar observations into understandable, location-specific disaster intelligence. Instead of simply displaying satellite images, the platform aims to combine multiple environmental indicators with machine learning and interactive 3D visualization to communicate potential risks.

Factors Considered

Our team considered satellite data availability, geographical complexity of the Himalayan terrain, rainfall patterns, slope conditions, data accuracy, computational requirements, accessibility, and the importance of providing understandable risk information. We also considered the need for a cost-effective and scalable solution that could be useful in disaster-prone regions.

Our vision is to bridge the gap between advanced satellite technology and real-world disaster preparedness, making Earth observation data more accessible, actionable, and meaningful for vulnerable communities.
